lesson.opening_patient_question: He was fine this morning. Why does he seem confused now?

course_objectives.text: Recognize clinical deterioration consistent with possible sepsis.

glossary.definition: Delivery of oxygenated blood to tissue; its failure is reported by several organ systems at once.
New confusion or reduced responsiveness compared with the patient's earlier state.
A perfusion-related change in an organ system that differs from this patient's own baseline.
Activating the organisation's sepsis or rapid-response pathway, communicating trend and suspected source, obtaining ordered diagnostics, and beginning stabilization.
Coordinating diagnostics, treatment and stabilization together rather than waiting for one step to finish.

slides.slide_title: From suspicion to escalation
slides.learning_objective: Orient to the lesson's promise.
on_slide_text: Early recognition and escalation of sepsis
Prelicensure RN · Physiological Adaptation · high safety risk
slides.speaker_script: This lesson is about a patient who might have an infection and is beginning to change. By the end you can name the changes that mean the body is failing to perfuse, say what the nurse does first, and describe how to tell whether it worked. This is a high-risk topic: the cost of noticing late is measured in organs.

slides.slide_title: Opening case: the patient who got quiet
slides.learning_objective: Enter the lesson through a patient whose only early cue is a change in mentation.
slides.visual_notes: Case card left, cues centre, task right.
slides.speaker_script: Here is your patient. Treated for an infection, stable this morning, and now different. The nurse who walks in says the patient seems confused, and the blood pressure is lower than it has been. Nothing here is dramatic. There is no alarm. Notice what you already want to do with this information, and hold on to it: we will come back to this patient at the end and see whether your first instinct was the safe one.

card_data.presentation: Treated for a suspected infection. Stable this morning. The nurse reports that the patient now seems confused, and the blood pressure is below the patient's trend for the shift.
cues: New confusion in a previously oriented patient
Blood pressure below this patient's own trend
Not yet known: source, urine output, perfusion elsewhere
card_data.prompt: Thirty seconds: is this a call-now change or a watch-and-recheck change?

slides.slide_title: The question this lesson answers
slides.learning_objective: State the organizing clinical question.
slides.speaker_script: One question organizes everything that follows. A patient who might have an infection is changing: which changes mean the body is failing to perfuse, and what does the nurse do before anything else? Five lanes carry the answer, from what normal looks like through to whether your action worked.

slides.slide_title: Lesson map: normal, changed, meaning, act, check
slides.learning_objective: Locate any sepsis cue on the map before acting on it.
slides.visual_notes: Horizontal route, foundation left to evaluation right.
slides.speaker_script: Map first. Normal on the left, the check on the right. Every cue you meet today belongs somewhere on this line, and knowing where it sits tells you what to do with it.

slides.slide_title: Warm-up: what has to happen first?
slides.learning_objective: Sequence the nurse's actions before seeing the answer.
on_slide_text: Reassess and trend the response
Notice a change in a patient who might have an infection
Activate the pathway and begin stabilization
Ask whether the change indicates organ dysfunction
slides.activity_prompt: Place the four actions in order.
answer_key: notice the change
ask whether it indicates organ dysfunction
activate the pathway and begin stabilization
reassess and trend the response
slides.speaker_script: One minute. Put these four in the order the nurse actually performs them. Do not overthink it, and do not look ahead. Compare with a neighbour before the reveal. The order matters more than the words.

slides.slide_title: Baseline: what perfusion is for
slides.learning_objective: Explain why a perfusion failure shows up in several systems at once.
on_slide_text: Perfusion delivers oxygen to tissue
Organs announce failure in their own language
Compare against this patient's own trend, not a textbook number
slides.visual_notes: Four organ cards, one cue each.
slides.speaker_script: Before cues make sense, hold on to why they cluster. Perfusion is the delivery of oxygen to tissue. When delivery falls, every organ that depends on it starts to complain, and each one complains in its own language: the brain becomes confused, the kidney makes less urine, the lungs work harder. That is why sepsis is recognised as a pattern across systems rather than as one abnormal number. And the comparison that matters is with this patient's own earlier readings, not with a population normal.

card_data.heading: Brain
card_data.body: Altered mentation: new confusion, less responsive than earlier.

card_data.heading: Kidney
card_data.body: Reduced urine output.

card_data.heading: Lungs
card_data.body: Respiratory change.

card_data.heading: Circulation
card_data.body: Abnormal perfusion; hypotension.

slides.slide_title: Cues: the five the module names
slides.learning_objective: Name the cue families that, with possible infection, require urgent assessment.
on_slide_text: Possible infection PLUS any new organ dysfunction
Altered mentation · abnormal perfusion · respiratory change
Hypotension · reduced urine output
Any other new organ dysfunction counts
slides.speaker_script: Here is the recognition rule in full. Possible infection, plus altered mentation, abnormal perfusion, respiratory change, hypotension, reduced urine output, or other new organ dysfunction, requires urgent assessment. Read the word 'or' carefully. You are not waiting to collect the set. One new organ dysfunction in a patient who might be infected is the trigger.

card_data.heading: Altered mentation
card_data.body: New confusion or reduced responsiveness.

card_data.heading: Abnormal perfusion
card_data.body: Skin and circulatory findings that differ from this patient's earlier state.

card_data.heading: Respiratory change
card_data.body: A new change in the work or rate of breathing.

card_data.heading: Hypotension
card_data.body: Blood pressure below this patient's trend.

card_data.heading: Reduced urine output
card_data.body: Less urine than earlier in the shift.

card_data.heading: Other new organ dysfunction
card_data.body: The list is not a closed set.

slides.slide_title: Activity: match the cue to the organ it speaks for
slides.learning_objective: Match each observed cue to the system whose perfusion it reports on.
slides.activity_prompt: Write A-? B-? C-? D-? and one sentence saying what the match tells you about perfusion.
answer_key: A-2 new confusion reports on cerebral perfusion
B-3 falling urine output reports on renal perfusion
C-1 rising respiratory rate reports on the lungs and on compensation
D-4 hypotension reports on circulatory failure to maintain pressure
slides.speaker_script: Work with one partner. Match each cue on the left to the system it reports on. This is not trivia: naming the system is what turns a number into a statement about perfusion, and that is the step that makes you escalate.

left: A. New confusion in a previously oriented patient
B. Urine output falling across the shift
D. Blood pressure below the patient's trend

slides.slide_title: Debrief: why naming the system changes what you do
slides.learning_objective: Explain how each match raises or lowers urgency.
slides.speaker_script: Here is the reasoning behind each match. Notice that in every row the cue is only meaningful because it is new. A patient with long-standing renal impairment and a low urine output is telling you something different from the patient whose output fell this afternoon. New is the word that carries the urgency.

card_data.heading: A to 2 · brain
card_data.body: New confusion in possible infection is organ dysfunction, not just an anxious patient.

card_data.heading: B to 3 · kidney
card_data.body: Falling output suggests the kidney is not being perfused.

card_data.heading: C to 1 · lungs
card_data.body: A rising rate is often the earliest visible compensation.

card_data.heading: D to 4 · circulation
card_data.body: Hypotension means compensation is no longer keeping up.

slides.slide_title: Trend beats any single value
slides.learning_objective: Justify using the trend rather than one reading.
on_slide_text: One value is a snapshot; the trend is the story
Combined movement in several systems raises urgency
A value inside the normal range can still be a change
slides.speaker_script: This is the discipline the module keeps returning to: trend changes rather than relying on one value. A single reading tells you where the patient is. Two readings tell you where the patient is going, and direction is what decides urgency. Two findings moving together, such as urine output falling while heart rate and respiratory rate rise, are a stronger signal than any one of them alone.

card_data.label: single value
card_data.event: a snapshot; may sit inside the normal range

slides.slide_title: Checkpoint: the patient with a normal temperature
slides.learning_objective: Reject the assumption that a normal temperature excludes sepsis.
answer_key: C. Continue evaluating for sepsis using the complete clinical picture and organ-function findings.
slides.speaker_script: One question, and it targets the most common misconception in this topic. Read the options and commit before the reveal.

card_data.stem: A patient has a possible infection but a temperature within the normal range. What is the best nursing response?
options: A. Document the normal temperature and recheck at the next scheduled vitals.
B. Rule out sepsis, since fever is required for the diagnosis.
C. Continue evaluating for sepsis using the complete clinical picture and organ-function findings.
D. Wait for the culture result before assessing further.
card_data.rationale: A normal temperature does not exclude serious infection or sepsis. The evaluation rests on the whole picture and on organ-function findings, not on one vital sign.

slides.slide_title: Meaning: new organ dysfunction raises urgency
slides.learning_objective: State the rule that converts a cue into an escalation.
on_slide_text: Possible infection + new organ dysfunction = urgent
The dysfunction does not have to be severe, only new
Absence of fever does not lower the urgency
slides.speaker_script: The conversion rule is short. Possible infection plus new organ dysfunction requires urgent assessment. Two words carry the weight. 'New' rules out the chronic finding you already knew about. 'Organ dysfunction' rules in the brain, the kidney, the lungs and the circulation, whichever of them is speaking. Nothing in that rule mentions temperature.

card_data.heading: New
card_data.body: Different from this patient's own earlier state.

card_data.heading: Organ dysfunction
card_data.body: Any system reporting a perfusion failure.

card_data.heading: Together
card_data.body: With possible infection, the two together mean urgent assessment now.

slides.slide_title: Escalate: what the nurse actually does
slides.learning_objective: List the four components of escalation named by the module.
on_slide_text: Activate the organisation's sepsis or rapid-response pathway
Communicate the trend and the suspected source
Obtain ordered diagnostics promptly
Begin stabilization
slides.visual_notes: Four cards, equal weight, no arrows: these are concurrent.
slides.speaker_script: Escalation is four things, and the module lists them as one movement rather than a sequence. Activate your organisation's sepsis or rapid-response pathway. Communicate the trend and the suspected source, not just the latest number. Obtain the ordered diagnostics promptly. And begin stabilization. Notice that the pathway is your organisation's: this lesson does not tell you which one, because that is local.

card_data.heading: Activate
card_data.body: The organisation's sepsis or rapid-response pathway.

card_data.heading: Communicate
card_data.body: The trend and the suspected source.

card_data.heading: Obtain
card_data.body: Ordered diagnostics, promptly.

card_data.heading: Begin
card_data.body: Stabilization.

slides.slide_title: Escalation and stabilization happen together
slides.learning_objective: Reject the sequential reading in which one step waits for another.
on_slide_text: Deterioration requires parallel action
Do not wait passively for one step to finish
Diagnostics and treatment are coordinated, not queued
slides.speaker_script: This is the slide that most often changes practice. When cultures and treatment are pending and the patient is deteriorating, the nurse coordinates time-sensitive diagnostics and treatment while continuing stabilization and escalation. Deterioration requires parallel action rather than waiting passively for one step to finish. The sequential habit -- order it, wait for it, then act -- is the one to unlearn here.

card_data.label: recognise
card_data.event: possible infection plus new organ dysfunction

card_data.label: reassess
card_data.event: continuous, not at the next scheduled check

slides.slide_title: What you hand over when you escalate
slides.learning_objective: Compose an escalation message carrying trend and suspected source.
on_slide_text: The trend, not only the latest value
The suspected source of infection
Which organ systems are involved
What you have already begun
slides.activity_prompt: Say it aloud in two sentences: trend, then suspected source.
answer_key: Sentence one names what has changed and in which direction, across which systems.
Sentence two names the suspected source and what has already been started.
slides.visual_notes: Four cards; the first two are the module's, the last two are instructor additions.
slides.speaker_script: When you make the call, the content matters. The module asks for the trend and the suspected source. That means the receiving clinician hears where the patient is going and why you think there is an infection, rather than a single number out of context. Add which systems are involved and what you have already started, so no one repeats your work.

card_data.heading: Trend
card_data.body: What has changed, in which direction, over what period.

card_data.heading: Suspected source
card_data.body: Why infection is suspected.

card_data.heading: Systems
card_data.body: Which organs are reporting dysfunction.

card_data.heading: Already begun
card_data.body: Diagnostics obtained, stabilization started.

slides.slide_title: Sort by urgency: which of these calls now?
slides.learning_objective: Sort findings by whether they require immediate escalation.
slides.activity_prompt: Place each finding in a column and justify one of them.
answer_key: Escalate now: new confusion with possible infection; hypotension below the patient's trend; falling urine output with rising heart and respiratory rate
Assess and keep trending: a single reading at the edge of normal with no change from baseline; a long-standing finding that has not changed
slides.speaker_script: Drag these mentally into two columns. The left column is escalate now. The right is assess and keep trending. The test for the left column is the rule from slide twelve: possible infection plus something new.

categories.title: Escalate now
items: Urine output falling while heart and respiratory rates rise

categories.title: Assess and keep trending
items: One value at the edge of normal, unchanged from baseline
A chronic finding that has not moved

slides.slide_title: Mini case: the patient who does not improve
slides.learning_objective: Choose the response when the first intervention has not worked.
slides.activity_prompt: Write two sentences: one assessment sentence, one escalation sentence.
answer_key: Assessment names perfusion and the trend since the intervention.
Escalation states that hypotension persists and requests higher-level support.
slides.speaker_script: Back to a bedside. Initial interventions are done and the blood pressure has not come up. Three columns: what you assess, what you say, and the error to avoid. Write a two-sentence response before the debrief.

card_data.presentation: Blood pressure remains low after initial interventions for suspected sepsis.
cues: Assess: perfusion, mentation, urine output, and the full trend since the intervention
Escalate: report immediately that hypotension persists; keep reassessing response
Avoid: reading a completed intervention as a resolved problem
card_data.prompt: Write two sentences: one assessment sentence, one escalation sentence.

slides.slide_title: Capstone: choose the next safe action
slides.learning_objective: Select the priority response to persistent hypotension after intervention.
answer_key: B. Escalate immediately and continue reassessing perfusion and treatment response.
slides.speaker_script: One question. It is the same patient from the mini case, and the options are all things a nurse might plausibly do.

card_data.scenario: Blood pressure remains low after initial interventions. The patient is more difficult to rouse than an hour ago.
card_data.stem: What is the priority nursing action?
options: A. Recheck the blood pressure in thirty minutes to confirm the trend before calling.
B. Escalate immediately and continue reassessing perfusion and treatment response.
C. Document that interventions were completed as ordered and continue the current plan.
D. Reposition the patient and repeat the reading in the other arm before escalating.
card_data.rationale: Persistent hypotension indicates ongoing instability and the need for higher-level support. A, C and D all delay escalation while the patient continues to deteriorate; the added difficulty rousing the patient is a second organ system reporting.

slides.slide_title: Rapid retrieval: five-item exit check
slides.learning_objective: Retrieve one point per lane without notes.
on_slide_text: Name three of the cue families that pair with possible infection
Which single word makes a finding count as organ dysfunction?
Does a normal temperature reduce your concern? Why not?
Name the four components of escalation
What does persistent hypotension after intervention tell you?
answer_key: any three of: altered mentation, abnormal perfusion, respiratory change, hypotension, reduced urine output, other new organ dysfunction
'new' -- different from this patient's own earlier state
no; a normal temperature does not exclude serious infection or sepsis
activate the pathway, communicate trend and suspected source, obtain ordered diagnostics, begin stabilization
ongoing instability and the need for higher-level support; escalate and keep reassessing
slides.speaker_script: Five questions, one per lane, answered aloud or on paper. If a lane produces silence, that is the lane to remediate before this cohort meets a real one.

slides.slide_title: Takeaway: notice, name, act together, check again
slides.learning_objective: Carry one frame to the bedside.
on_slide_text: Notice: any new organ dysfunction in possible infection
Name: which system, and in which direction
Act together: escalate and stabilize in parallel
Check again: reassess, and escalate again if it persists
slides.speaker_script: Closing frame. The patient from the opening case had one cue and no alarm. That is what this looks like in real life.

card_data.title: notice
card_data.body: possible infection plus anything new

card_data.title: name
card_data.body: which system is reporting, and which way it is moving

card_data.title: act together
card_data.body: pathway, communication, diagnostics and stabilization, in parallel

card_data.title: check again
card_data.body: trend the response; persistent deterioration escalates again

assessment_items.learning_objective: Recognize clinical deterioration consistent with possible sepsis.
assessment_items.stem: A patient being treated for a suspected infection develops new confusion, and the blood pressure is below the patient's trend for the shift. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: A. Activate urgent sepsis evaluation and assess airway, breathing, circulation, and perfusion.
B. Reorient the patient and recheck the blood pressure at the next scheduled vitals.
C. Request a sedation review, since new confusion is most often medication-related.
D. Obtain a repeat blood pressure in the opposite arm before taking further action.
assessment_items.rationale: Possible infection with new organ dysfunction and hypotension requires immediate escalation. B and D delay recognition of a time-sensitive change; C attributes a perfusion cue to a cause not supported by the picture.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.learning_objective: Recognize clinical deterioration consistent with possible sepsis.
assessment_items.stem: Over one shift a patient's urine output falls while the heart rate and respiratory rate rise. How should the nurse interpret this combination?
options: A. The findings are unrelated and should be charted separately.
B. The combined trend can signal worsening organ perfusion and should be reported promptly.
C. The rising respiratory rate is the only finding that requires action.
D. The findings are expected after a period of reduced oral intake and require no escalation.
assessment_items.rationale: The combined trend can signal worsening organ perfusion; the nurse reports the deterioration promptly and reassesses perfusion and the full vital-sign trend. Reading the findings separately, or attributing them to intake, loses the pattern that carries the urgency.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.learning_objective: Recognize clinical deterioration consistent with possible sepsis.
assessment_items.stem: A patient has a possible infection but a temperature within the normal range. What should the nurse do?
options: A. Rule out sepsis, since fever is required for the diagnosis.
B. Continue evaluating for sepsis using the complete clinical picture and organ-function findings.
C. Defer further assessment until a fever develops.
D. Treat the normal temperature as evidence that the infection is resolving.
assessment_items.rationale: A normal temperature does not exclude serious infection or sepsis. Evaluation continues on the complete clinical picture and the organ-function findings.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.stem: Ordered cultures and treatment are pending while a patient with suspected sepsis continues to deteriorate. Which action best reflects safe practice?
options: A. Wait for the culture result before beginning any further intervention.
B. Complete the diagnostics first, then begin stabilization once results return.
C. Coordinate time-sensitive diagnostics and treatment while continuing stabilization and escalation.
D. Hold escalation until the full set of ordered tests has been collected.
assessment_items.rationale: Deterioration requires parallel action rather than waiting passively for one step to finish. A, B and D all treat the steps as a queue, which delays both diagnosis and treatment in a time-sensitive presentation.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.stem: Blood pressure remains low after initial interventions for suspected sepsis. What does this finding indicate, and what should the nurse do?
options: A. The interventions need more time; continue the current plan and recheck at the next scheduled vitals.
B. Persistent hypotension indicates ongoing instability; escalate immediately and continue reassessing perfusion and response.
C. The reading is likely inaccurate; repeat it before reporting anything.
D. Document that the ordered interventions were completed and hand over at the end of the shift.
assessment_items.rationale: Persistent hypotension indicates ongoing instability and the need for higher-level support. The other options all delay escalation while the patient remains under-perfused.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.learning_objective: Recognize clinical deterioration consistent with possible sepsis.
assessment_items.stem: A patient is being treated for a possible infection. Which new findings should prompt urgent assessment for sepsis? Select all that apply.
options: A. New confusion in a previously oriented patient
B. Reduced urine output compared with earlier in the shift
C. A long-standing finding that has not changed
D. A new respiratory change
E. Blood pressure below this patient's own trend
assessment_items.rationale: Altered mentation, reduced urine output, respiratory change and hypotension are all named cue families, and each counts when it is new. C fails the test that makes a finding count: it is not new.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.stem: A nurse is escalating a patient with suspected sepsis. Which actions belong to escalation as described in this lesson? Select all that apply.
options: A. Activate the organisation's sepsis or rapid-response pathway
B. Communicate the trend and the suspected source
C. Obtain the ordered diagnostics promptly
D. Begin stabilization
E. Wait for the rapid-response team before starting anything
assessment_items.rationale: The module names activation, communication of trend and suspected source, prompt diagnostics, and beginning stabilization. E contradicts the parallel-action principle.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

assessment_items.stem: Which set of findings should the nurse trend when evaluating a patient's response to treatment for suspected sepsis?
options: A. Temperature alone, since it reflects the infection most directly.
B. Mental status, perfusion, blood pressure, oxygenation, urine output, laboratory results, and response to treatment.
C. Blood pressure alone, since hypotension drove the escalation.
D. Whatever was abnormal at the time of escalation, and nothing further.
assessment_items.rationale: Evaluation trends mental status, perfusion, blood pressure, oxygenation, urine output, laboratory results and response to treatment, and escalates persistent deterioration. Narrowing to one value repeats the single-value error the lesson warns against.
assessment_items.origin: keyed action and rationale from the SRC02 topic's facts[]; distractors instructor-written (the module's shared distractors repeat across all items)

defects.note: [clinical specificity] SRC02 states cues qualitatively and names no numeric thresholds, no scoring tool, and no bundle timing. This lesson deliberately adds none. If the programme teaches specific criteria or a local pathway, the author adds them; they are not inferable from the source and were not invented here.

[assessment] SRC02's facts[] share one set of three distractors, identical across all five facts and all implausible. Reused as written they would teach test-taking rather than clinical judgement, so distractors here are instructor-written; each keyed action and rationale is the module's. Author to review the replacements.

[evidence] All clinical slides are source-aligned to SRC02 (the author's own module), not source-grounded. No OpenStax text is reproduced; the module's upstream OpenStax citation remains excluded pending the license contradiction check.
[instructor-added] The 'systems' and 'already begun' handover cards extend the module's two named elements (trend, suspected source). Confirm against local handover convention.
[standards] Package-level CA-BRN-ART3 refs BRN-14 and BRN-17 are proposed by the builder; author to confirm before any compliance filing. Slide-level standards_refs left empty.
